newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Royal Bank of Scotland head seeks one yr EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Royal Bank of Scotland head seeks one yr EMU delay.

text.p: The chairman of the Royal Bank of Scotland Group, Lord Younger, said on Tuesday the launch of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) should be delayed by 12 months to give member states time to get their economies in shape.

"I don't think they will do it, but it would be very wise for (German) Chancellor (Helmut) Kohl and co. to agree to a delay of the launch because I think the economic convergence would be so much easier with another 12 months to go," Younger told Reuters.

Younger, a former British Conservative government minister, told Reuters he had always been puzzled by the theory that postponement of EMU's planned launch date on 1 January 1999 would necessarily cause mayhem on foreign exchange markets.

"It is certainly true that if there were a delay and it was interpreted as possibly a stop (to EMU), then that would" (cause foreign exchange market instability), said Younger, who was attending a banking conference.

"But if they did have a delay, which I don't think they will, they would surely accompany it by a very robust restatement of the fact that 'this is merely a 12-month delay - we are going ahead etc'," Younger said.

"I think they are hell-bent on going ahead on time, which I suppose is good for progress towards (EMU) but it is very difficult for the robustness of the economic convergence which is not yet good enough."

Former Conservative prime minister John Major also said on Tuesday the launch of EMU should be postponed in the light of the Socialist win in France's parliamentary elections and the argument between the German government and the Bundesbank over Kohl's plan to revalue Germany's gold reserves.
Younger said the British Labour party's victory at elections last month made British participation in EMU "slightly more likely and slightly sooner than it might otherwise be".

Asked whether Britain might yet decide to join EMU at the outset, Younger said this was "very unlikely still but slightly less unlikely than it was before the election". But the situation would be different if EMU itself were postponed.

Lord Alexander, chairman of NatWest Group, said there was now a greater risk that the euro might be a soft currency, whereas it was important that it should be as hard as possible in the interests of good economic management.

"I think the likelihood is that as a result of the French elections, if EMU happens, it will be a broader EMU than looked likely a few months ago," Alexander added. -- Stephen Nisbet, Zurich editorial +411 631 7340
